sources.claim: Browser DevTools expose sources, breakpoints, network, console, DOM, storage, and performance evidence for one runtime state.

canonicalExplanation.summary: DevTools lets you **watch your program run**. The **Sources** panel shows your files; click a line number to set a **breakpoint** — execution pauses there so you can read every variable. Step over, into and out of functions to follow the flow. The **Console** is a live REPL on the running page: it can read *and change* state, so use it deliberately. Once you find a bug, keep a **regression test** so it can't return.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A "Mark lesson complete" button sometimes marks the wrong lesson. Adding `console.log` everywhere floods the Console. Instead, pause the program at the exact moment of the click and look. A breakpoint confirms an event payload before code is changed, and a regression test preserves the finding. In this lesson you'll use developer tools to locate and explain a state-transition defect.

```predict
{"question": "You type `state.completed = []` in the Console while the app runs. What happens?", "options": ["Nothing — the Console only prints", "The running app's state really changes"], "answer": 1, "why": "The Console runs code in the page. That's powerful for experiments — and a reason to be careful."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Source-to-execution models**, **Standards-mode document skeleton**, **Scripts and console**, and **Debugging and testing loop** (reproduce, hypothesise, observe, fix, test).

sections.heading: The model: pause, inspect, step
sections.body:
| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| line breakpoint. | pause before a line runs. |
| conditional breakpoint. | pause only when an expression is true (e.g. `id === 7`). |
| `debugger;` statement. | a breakpoint written in code (remove before committing). |
| Scope pane. | local, closure and global variables at the pause. |
| Call stack. | which functions led here. |
| step over / into / out. | run the next line / enter a call / finish the current function. |
| Console. | evaluate expressions in the paused scope. |

```js
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const id = Number(event.target.dataset.lessonId);  // ← breakpoint here
  markComplete(id);
});
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "What would you check first at that breakpoint?", "answer": "`event.target` — is it the button, or a child span inside it? If a span, `dataset.lessonId` is undefined, so id becomes NaN."}
```

sections.heading: Keep the finding

includes: Set line and conditional breakpoints, step through code and read scope and call stack.
Use the Console carefully and preserve findings with regression tests.

outcomes: Use developer tools to locate and explain a state-transition defect.

examples.title: Pausing on a click to read the payload
examples.situation: A breakpoint confirms an event payload before code is changed and a regression test preserves the finding.
walkthrough: **Breakpoint:** set on the `const id = …` line and click the icon inside the button.
**Confirm the event payload:** Scope shows `event.target` is the `<span class="icon">`, whose `dataset.lessonId` is undefined → id is NaN.
**Fix and test:** use `event.target.closest("[data-lesson-id]")`; a regression test that will click the inner span now passes.
examples.result: The right lesson is marked every time, and a test guards the fix.

examples.title: The counter that skipped numbers
examples.situation: A step counter sometimes jumps by 2. Console logs show nothing obvious.
walkthrough: A breakpoint in the increment function is hit twice for a single click.
The call stack shows the function called from two event listeners — one added on every render.
Fix: register the listener once; add a test that renders twice and clicks once, expecting +1.
examples.result: The counter increments by exactly one, and the duplicated-listener cause is documented by a test.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The console is only for printing and cannot alter application behaviour.
misconceptions.correction: The Console evaluates JavaScript in the running page, so it can read and change state, call functions and trigger requests. Use it deliberately — ideally while paused at a breakpoint in the right scope.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what did typing in the Console do?

analogy.example: Debugging with breakpoints is like **pausing a match replay**: freeze the exact moment, look at every player's position (variables), then advance frame by frame (step). console.log is like reading the scoreboard afterwards.
limitations: Replays can't be changed; the Console can change live state.
A regression test is like adding the play to the training plan.

steps.explanation: The breakpoint pauses on the click handler before any code changes.
The breakpoint confirms an event payload that explains the wrong mark.
A regression test preserves the finding after the fix.

trace.textAlternative: Debugging a click handler. Step 1, Pause: paused at is const id line; event.target is span.icon. The breakpoint pauses on the click handler before any code changes. Step 2, Inspect payload: dataset.lessonId is undefined; id is NaN. The breakpoint confirms an event payload that explains the wrong mark. Step 3, Fix and test: target is closest('[data-lesson-id]'); regression test is passes. A regression test preserves the finding after the fix.

nearTransfer.prompt: A function returns the wrong total only for the 5th item. Which breakpoint type do you use, and what condition?
expectedEvidence: A conditional breakpoint in the loop.

farTransfer.prompt: Pick a bug in your own project. Reproduce it, pause at the right moment with a breakpoint, record variable values and call stack, fix it, and add a regression test.
expectedEvidence: A regression test that fails before and passes after the fix.

remediation.explanation: Before editing code: **reproduce → set a breakpoint where the wrong value first appears → read Scope and Call Stack → write the cause in one sentence.** Then fix and add a test.
remediation.retryPrompt: Follow this for "The counter that skipped numbers".

recap.summary: To locate and explain a state-transition defect, pause at a breakpoint (line or conditional), inspect scope, event payload and call stack, step through the change, use the Console carefully, and keep a regression test for the finding.
retrievalPrompts: What does the Scope pane show?
Can the Console change app state?
Why add a regression test after debugging?
